description: Evacuation, the Blitz, rationing, women in industry and the propaganda war on the home front.
content_html:
Preparing for War

From 1937 onwards, the British government began planning for a war it hoped to avoid. Air Raid Precautions (ARP) were established, and by September 1939 every household had received a gas mask. Millions of Anderson shelters — corrugated steel structures half-buried in gardens — were distributed free to households with incomes below a set level. Blackout regulations required all windows to be covered after dark so that enemy bombers could not identify towns from the air.

When war was declared on 3 September 1939, the government immediately began evacuation. In the first three days, approximately 1.5 million children were moved from cities to rural areas, separated from their families and billeted with strangers. For many urban children it was their first encounter with the countryside. The experience was mixed: some children found kind hosts and new opportunities; others faced difficult conditions or simply ran away home. A second wave of evacuation followed during the Blitz in 1940–1941.

Key Fact

In the first three days after war was declared in September 1939, approximately 1.5 million children were evacuated from British cities to rural areas. Experiences varied enormously: some children found caring hosts and benefited from country life; others faced hardship or returned home without permission.

The Blitz

From September 1940 to May 1941, German bombers attacked British cities in what became known as the Blitz. London was bombed on 57 consecutive nights from 7 September 1940. Other cities including Coventry, Birmingham, Liverpool, Bristol, Plymouth and Glasgow were also heavily targeted. The Coventry raid of 14 November 1940, in which over 500 bombers dropped incendiary and high-explosive bombs, destroyed the medieval city centre and killed approximately 554 people.

The Blitz killed approximately 43,000 British civilians and made around one million people homeless. Londoners sheltered in Underground stations, basements and purpose-built shelters. The government promoted an image of the “Blitz spirit” — ordinary people enduring hardship with stoicism and good humour. While there was genuine community solidarity, historians have also noted that the reality included looting, panic and a significant toll on mental health. The East End of London, where working-class communities lived near the docks, suffered disproportionately compared with wealthier areas.

The wartime government and the BBC promoted the “Blitz spirit” narrative — images of cheerful cockneys singing in shelters, shopkeepers hanging “Business as Usual” signs in bombed windows. This narrative was partly genuine: crime rates did not rise dramatically, community mutual aid was widespread, and many people displayed remarkable resilience. However, censorship suppressed news of panicking crowds, looting and the psychological breakdown of some individuals. Churchill personally visited the East End to be seen among the people. Historians such as Angus Calder in The Myth of the Blitz (1991) have argued that the “Blitz spirit” story was partly constructed to serve morale, and that class inequalities — wealthier families leaving cities, poorer families having no choice but to stay — were glossed over.

Rationing

Rationing was introduced in January 1940, initially for butter, sugar and bacon. By 1942, most foods, clothing and petrol were rationed. Ration books were issued to every person; shops would stamp a book when the week’s allowance was used. The weekly ration for a typical adult included 4 oz of bacon, 2 oz of butter, and 2 oz of cheese — quantities that seem tiny by modern standards but which, combined with unrationed foods, kept the population adequately fed.

Paradoxically, the war years improved the health of many working-class Britons. Rationing ensured the poorest families received a guaranteed minimum of protein and calories — better than many had managed during the Depression. The government introduced the “Dig for Victory” campaign, encouraging people to grow vegetables in parks and gardens. The “British Restaurant” scheme provided cheap hot meals in community canteens. Rationing continued well after the war ended: meat was not fully derationed until 1954.

Key Fact

Food rationing began in January 1940 with butter, sugar and bacon, and expanded to cover most foods and clothing by 1942. Although hardship was genuine, rationing actually improved nutrition among poorer families compared with the Depression years. Rationing did not fully end until 1954.

Women’s Roles in Wartime

As in the First World War, women’s labour became essential to the war effort. However, the Second World War went further: the National Service Act of 1941 made all unmarried women aged 20–30 liable to conscription into the women’s auxiliary services or essential war work. Women worked in aircraft factories, on the railways, in the land army farming the countryside, and in the armed forces’ support services (the ATS, WRNS and WAAF). By 1943, around 7.75 million women were in paid employment or the auxiliary services.

Women’s wartime roles challenged pre-war assumptions about what women could do. Factory managers who had doubted women’s ability to operate machinery found them capable and productive. However, women consistently earned less than men for the same work — a grievance that would resurface in the post-war years. When the war ended, many women were expected to return to domestic roles as returning male veterans reclaimed jobs. The experience of wartime work nonetheless contributed to longer-term changes in women’s expectations and aspirations.

The Ministry of Information, established at the outbreak of war, controlled the flow of news and produced posters, films and radio broadcasts to maintain public morale and shape behaviour. Famous campaigns included “Careless Talk Costs Lives” (warning against discussing troop movements), “Dig for Victory” and “Make Do and Mend.” The BBC became the trusted voice of wartime Britain: its news bulletins were heard across Europe by occupied populations as well as British audiences. The government balanced censorship with enough honest reporting to maintain public trust — early wartime disasters (such as the fall of France in 1940) were reported, if carefully framed. Documentary films like Listen to Britain (1942) celebrated ordinary resilience.
exam_tip_html: On a 5-mark ‘Source Utility’ question, always address three elements: the content of the source (what information it actually gives), the provenance (who produced it, when, and why — which affects its reliability and purpose), and your own contextual knowledge (what you know that helps judge how useful the source is for the specific enquiry). A common mistake is spending all your answer describing the source’s content and ignoring provenance — this caps your marks below the top band.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Blitz (September 1940 – May 1941) killed approximately 43,000 civilians and made around a million homeless; the government’s “Blitz spirit” narrative celebrated resilience while censoring evidence of breakdown and inequality.
  • Rationing began in January 1940, eventually covering most food and clothing; paradoxically it improved nutrition among the poorest compared with Depression-era privation, and did not fully end until 1954.
  • Women were conscripted into war work from 1941, with around 7.75 million in employment or auxiliary services by 1943; wartime roles expanded expectations even though women still earned less than men and many returned to domestic life after 1945.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the evacuation programme that began in September 1939.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for any one well-described feature, for example:
• Approximately 1.5 million children were moved from cities to rural areas in the first three days.
• Children were separated from their families and billeted with strangers in the countryside.
[2 marks: 1 for identifying the feature, 1 for describing it]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the government's rationing policy introduced from 1940.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for any two well-described features, for example:
• Rationing began in January 1940, initially covering butter, sugar and bacon, and expanded to most foods by 1942.
• Every person received a ration book stamped when the weekly allowance was used.
• Rationing improved nutrition among poorer families who had been underfed during the Depression.
• Food rationing did not fully end until 1954.
[4 marks: 2 marks per feature — 1 for identification, 1 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the introduction of rationing in Britain from 1940.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies the cause (threat to supply chains from German U-boat attacks on Atlantic convoys, or simply the need to ensure fair distribution of scarce goods during wartime) and develops the mechanism — imports reduced, government needed to ensure the whole population had a guaranteed minimum, prevent hoarding, and maintain morale.
Secure: Names a clear cause and provides a linked explanation with some development.
Developing: Names a relevant cause with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague reference to wartime shortages without identifying a specific cause.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Blitz for the people of Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a consequence (e.g. approximately 43,000 civilian deaths and one million made homeless, or the growth of community solidarity and the “Blitz spirit”) and develops a chain — the scale of civilian casualties transformed the war into a people’s conflict, forced the government to address working-class grievances, contributed to demand for post-war social reform.
Secure: Clear identification and explanation with development.
Developing: Names a consequence with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague reference without explanation.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the role of women on the Home Front during the Second World War.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Addresses significance at the time (conscription from 1941, 7.75 million women in work/auxiliary services by 1943, demonstrated capability in factory and military support roles) AND over time (contributed to changing expectations, fuelled later demands for equal pay, influenced post-war women's roles and eventually legislation). Weighs limits — lower pay than men, many returned to domestic roles post-1945.
Secure: Addresses both dimensions with clear explanation.
Developing: One dimension only with some explanation.
Emerging: Describes women's roles without analysing significance.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Propaganda was the most important way the government kept up morale during the Second World War.' How far do you agree? Use your knowledge to support or challenge this view.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument addressing propaganda (Ministry of Information, BBC, poster campaigns) alongside other factors (genuine community solidarity, rationing fairness, Churchill's leadership, shared sacrifice). Weighs factors with evidence. Reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence on propaganda and other factors. Some weighing. Structured conclusion.
Developing: Some relevant evidence but argument is unbalanced or conclusion underdeveloped.
Emerging: Descriptive account without sustained argument.
[16 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: From which month and year did German bombers begin the Blitz against British cities?
Which government body was responsible for wartime propaganda, including the 'Careless Talk Costs Lives' campaign?
Food _____ began in January 1940 and did not fully end until 1954.
In the first three days of the Second World War, approximately _____ million children were evacuated from British cities to rural areas.
Match each Home Front feature to its description:
right: Moving children from cities to rural areas for safety
Government system allocating fixed weekly food allowances via ration books
German bombing campaign against British cities, September 1940 to May 1941

flashcard_questions.q: What does ARP stand for, and when was it established?
Approximately how many children were evacuated from British cities in the first three days of the war?
The Blitz lasted from September 1940 to _____, killing approximately _____ civilians.
Which city was devastated in a single raid on 14 November 1940, with its medieval centre destroyed?
When did food rationing begin in Britain, and what was the very first item rationed?
flashcard_questions.a: Rationing began in January 1940, starting with butter, sugar and bacon before expanding to cover most foods by 1942.

flashcard_questions.q: When was the last food item derationed in Britain after the Second World War?
What did the National Service Act of 1941 do regarding women?
flashcard_questions.a: Made unmarried women aged 20-30 liable for conscription into auxiliary services or essential war work.

flashcard_questions.q: Approximately how many women were in paid employment or auxiliary services in Britain by 1943?
Which government body controlled news and produced morale-boosting propaganda during the war?
What was the 'Dig for Victory' campaign?
flashcard_questions.a: A government campaign encouraging people to grow vegetables in parks and gardens to supplement rationed food.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the term for the government shelter distributed to households at the start of the war?
How did wartime rationing affect the nutrition of the poorest British families?
flashcard_questions.a: It actually improved it by guaranteeing a minimum food allowance, better than many had during the Depression.

glossary_terms.definition: Civil defence preparations introduced from 1937 to protect civilians from air attack, including blackouts, shelters, gas masks and ARP wardens.
The wartime policy of moving children and vulnerable people from cities to safer rural areas to protect them from bombing.
The sustained German bombing campaign against British cities from September 1940 to May 1941, derived from the German word for lightning war.
The government system introduced from January 1940 to control the fair distribution of scarce food and other goods by issuing each person a fixed weekly allowance.
